summary: One of a series of surveys by David Smallberg checking which hosts accept connections for Telnet, FTP and mail over TCP. This edition tested hosts in January 1983. Replaced by RFC 842.

eli5.summary: Someone knocked on the door of every computer on the list to see which ones answered. This is the result for one week.

subtitle: An updated survey of TCP support on Internet hosts from January 1983.

tldr.problem: As the internet was rapidly changing, a single survey snapshot was already becoming outdated within weeks.
tldr.mechanism: Smallberg repeated the TCP connectivity test just one week after RFC 838, testing the same 323 hosts for Telnet, FTP, and SMTP support to measure how the network was evolving.
tldr.outcome: The new results show changes in TCP adoption: 182 hosts now accepted Telnet (up from 172), 165 accepted FTP (up from 159), and 159 accepted SMTP (up from 154). Some previously dead hosts were now reachable, indicating rapid infrastructure changes.

today: RFC 839 was obsoleted by RFC 842 just a few weeks later in February 1983. Like RFC 838, it serves as a historical snapshot of TCP deployment growth during the earliest years of the Internet.

sections.title: The Updated Survey
sections.content:
RFC 839 is the second in David Smallberg's series of TCP deployment surveys. Just one week after RFC 838, Smallberg ran the same test again on the same 323 hosts, testing from 25 January to 26 January 1983. This rapid re-testing provides valuable evidence of how quickly the Internet was changing and evolving during this early period.

By re-testing the same hosts only a week later, Smallberg captures a network in transition, with changes happening almost daily as more systems came online and previously offline machines were brought back up.
sections.eli5: One week after the first test, the tester knocked on the same doors again to see if anything had changed.

sections.title: Test Methodology
sections.content:
The testing procedure was identical to RFC 838. Smallberg used the same test host list from the NIC hostname table and tested for the same three services: Telnet, FTP, and SMTP. Like the previous survey, hosts that did not respond on the first attempt were retried the following day.

By using the same methodology, RFC 839 allows direct comparison with RFC 838, making it possible to track which specific hosts changed status and to measure the overall rate of TCP adoption across the network.
sections.eli5: He used the same test method as before, knocking on the same doors the same way.

sections.title: Updated Results
sections.content:
In one week, the results improved measurably. 182 hosts now accepted Telnet (compared to 172 the previous week), 165 accepted FTP (up from 159), and 159 accepted SMTP (up from 154). While 53 hosts were still dead (down from 66), the reliability of previously unreachable hosts also changed.

These week-to-week improvements suggest that the TCP infrastructure was maturing rapidly. Some hosts that had been down came back online, while others may have added TCP support. The data captures a moment when network infrastructure was growing faster than administrators could keep the central hostname table updated.
sections.eli5: More computers were now answering the knock. Telnet went from 172 to 182, FTP from 159 to 165, and SMTP from 154 to 159. That's progress in just one week.

sections.title: Week-to-Week Changes
sections.content:
The ability to compare RFC 838 and RFC 839 reveals important trends. Telnet adoption jumped by 10 hosts, FTP by 6, and SMTP by 5 in just one week. The total number of dead hosts fell from 66 to 53, suggesting that maintenance and upgrades were happening across the network.

However, the hostnames table claims also shifted, showing inconsistency in how administrators updated their metadata. This survey series demonstrates why a centralized way to discover and verify network services would eventually become important.
sections.eli5: Comparing the two weeks side by side shows that the network was fixing itself and growing. Dead computers came back to life, and more computers learned TCP.
